articles.title: The affordability election delivered billions for public transit
articles.content:
In an election dominated by concerns about affordability, voters across the country overwhelmingly agreed to raise taxes to preserve or expand public transit.

Out of 27 ballot measures supporting transit, 22 passed on November 3, representing $27.4 billion in funding to rescue faltering systems and expand or build new ones. Some of the biggest wins of the night included voters in the San Francisco Bay Area staving off enormous cuts to Bay Area Rapid Transit and other regional systems, Coloradans backing new regional rail, and residents of Seattle and nearby Pierce County favoring expanded bus service.

“It’s an indication that the public is willing to pay for these public transit improvements,” said Sohail Husain, a policy analyst at the Eno Center for Transportation. “That’s very telling –– especially in a world like today where people are concerned about affordability. I think people are still also concerned about mobility and having options to move.”

Public transit has now fared well in the red wave of 2024 — when 19 out of 25 measures supporting transit passed — and this year’s blue wave. Although few candidates campaigned on the issue, the results could significantly alter policy. At the state level, transit advocates see opportunities to advance projects or simply get the government out of the way. Meanwhile, a Democratic majority in Congress will shape a major transportation infrastructure law that is up for renewal. Together, the results could remake how Americans get around.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

States have broad discretion to fund transportation as they see fit, which is why Democratic wins in red states and Democratic control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in 22 states have many public transit advocates excited about what comes next.

Pennsylvania is one of those states. It has endured a bitter battle over the finances of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, which serves the Philadelphia area. When the agency faced 45 percent service cuts last year, Governor Josh Shapiro directed the state Department of Transportation to allow the agency to shift nearly $400 million from its capital to operational budget. He also made another $220 million available to the system.

Now, with Democrats taking control of both chambers of the state legislature, transit advocates say SEPTA can look beyond self-preservation. Stephen Bronskill of Transit Forward Philadelphia pointed to projects including trolley modernization, new fleets to replace vehicles from the 1970s, more frequent regional rail service, and fully accessible stations.

“This is a once-in-a-generation moment to invest in public transit –– safe, reliable, accessible transit that Philly needs, but all of Pennsylvania deserves,” he said.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The prospects are less straightforward in Texas, where Republicans still control the Senate. Jay Blazek Crossley, executive director of Farm&City, a nonprofit focused in part on road safety, has spent more than a decade trying to nudge GOP lawmakers toward less violent and less polluting transportation options. Every legislative session has seen him unsuccessfully push legislation that would make it easier for cities to reduce speed limits on residential streets. He sees new hope for that measure and, more broadly, a future that might include additional public transit funding, which accounts for just 0.72 percent of the transportation department’s budget. State Republicans have generally been more interested in moving more cars more quickly, primarily by building bigger highways, while pushing back against some city-led public transit efforts.

“At the very least, the state, I believe, will get out of the way on things like building good light rail and transit,” he said.

There’s hope for bigger projects too. State Representative John Bucy III has again filed legislation directing the Texas Department of Transportation to find a public-private partnership for a high-speed rail line linking Dallas and San Antonio. He believes the bill will appeal to lawmakers whose constituents would benefit from an alternative to driving on the heavily congested Interstate 35 corridor.

“I think the voters spoke loud and clear that they want a Texas government that is going to work on kitchen table issues,” he said. “I think that’s healthcare, education. It’s also mobility and transit, and how do we get around this big, vast state?”

Georgia is another state where Democrats took the governorship and flipped the House, but Republicans still control the Senate. That could be a challenge for Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who has called for dedicated state funding for the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority and other systems that have historically relied heavily on local and federal support.

The election could have even greater implications at the federal level, where Congress must soon decide how much spending to allocate to transit and passenger rail. The BUILD America 250 Act passed out of a key House commitee with bipartisan support in May, but left public transit advocates concerned about funding cuts. With Democrats taking control of Congress, the legislation is likely to look different. Representative Jerry Nadler of New York, the lone Democrat on the committee to oppose advancing the legislation, sees an opportunity to change its direction.

“Unlike the current Republican proposal, next year’s bill should not prioritize one mode of transportation at the expense of others. This bill must make robust investments in rail and public transit, to connect communities, create good-paying jobs, lower transportation costs for families, and reduce the cost of moving goods across the country,” he said in a statement.

But rewriting the bill won’t necessarily happen quickly. Rebecca Higgins, the Eno Center for Transportation’s vice president of policy, said lawmakers will face some urgency because Congress is already relying on an extension to fund transportation. At the same time, she expects lawmakers to give their newly elected colleagues a chance to weigh in. One major question is what happens to money for intercity passenger rail that was included in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act but dropped from BUILD America 250.

Whatever happens in Washington, the local and regional measures voters approved will have a more immediate impact. In the Bay Area, a 14-year regional sales tax is expected to raise about $1 billion annually to preserve service on BART and other systems that had been facing steep budget shortfalls. Colorado voters approved a 0.333 percent sales tax to build, operate, and maintain passenger rail connecting Pueblo and Colorado Springs with Denver and Fort Collins.

In Seattle, voters doubled an existing sales tax over the next decade, generating an additional $138 million per year largely for transit service. In nearby Pierce County, voters also approved a sales tax increase to expand bus service.

The Pierce County win is particularly notable because voters there hadn’t increased public transit investment since 2002, said Kirk Hovenkotter, the executive director of the Transportation Choices Coalition. The fast-growing region also faces an affordability crisis. The American Public Transportation Association estimates that relying on public transit rather than owning a car can save a household more than $14,000 annually.

Hovenkotter makes a similar argument about the costs facing residents of the Pacific Northweest. “The average cost of car ownership in Washington state is about $12,000,” he said. “The fastest way we can put $12,000 back in someone’s pocket is making it easier for them to live without a car or with one fewer car.”

The election results suggest that, for a wide swath of voters, transit funding isn’t competing with affordability concerns. It’s an answer to them.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant, positive real-world impact where voters across multiple states approved billions in funding to preserve and expand public transit systems. This has broad significance for the general public by improving mobility, reducing transportation costs, and potentially lowering environmental pollution. The article provides detailed context on various state-level measures, legislative prospects, and the expected benefits, making it a substantive and inspiring story about public transit investment and climate-friendly transportation.
articles.personality_title: Voters approve billions to improve public transit across the US
articles.personality_presentation:

articles.title: How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For decades, wastewater treatment plants have been filtering out bacteria, chemicals, and biological waste before discharging treated water back into the environment. Microplastics have been going straight through. This week, a plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to do something about that, installing […]
The post How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

For decades, wastewater treatment plants have been filtering out bacteria, chemicals, and biological waste before discharging treated water back into the environment. Microplastics have been going straight through. This week, a plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to do something about that, installing a system built specifically to capture microplastics before they reach the ocean. As of this moment, no law requires this. PolyGone Systems, a startup founded by two former Princeton University graduate students, built it anyway.

Why microplastics are hard to remove

Plastics don’t biodegrade; they break down into tinier and tinier fragments called microplastics, which don’t go away and build up in living organisms over time. Standard wastewater treatment removes a lot, but it wasn’t designed for particles this small or this plentiful. They get into the water from industrial discharge, stormwater picking up particles shed from car tires, and washing machines releasing microfibers from synthetic clothes. By the time water arrives at a treatment plant, the microplastics are already in it.

“We’re discharging to the ocean,” said Matt DeNafo, president of the Atlantic County Utilities Authority. “So, if we’re not removing the plastic that’s in our wastewater, we’re putting it back into the environment. It’s getting into the fish that we’re eating, even the water that we’re bathing. So, it really becomes an issue for human health.”

Microplastics and nanoplastics have already turned up in human bloodstream, brain tissue, and other organs. Some researchers have linked exposure to a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, though scientists are still working out exactly what harm these particles cause at different levels of exposure.

How the technology works

PolyGone’s founders, Nathaniel Banks and Yidian Liu, trained as architects, and the technology they built shows it. Their system, called Polypods, doesn’t try to filter microplastics out of water the conventional way. Instead, it replicates the surface of ultrahydrophobic plants found in wetlands, which microplastics cling to naturally. Scale that up, and you can pull microplastics out of a water stream with very little material and minimal energy.

The lab numbers are strong: more than 98 percent of microplastics removed. There’s no commercial data yet, but Banks and Liu say the Polypods work best on the smallest particles, which are also the hardest to catch by other means and the ones most easily absorbed by living tissue.

Liu on the design philosophy: “We really like how some sleek products such as the iPhone were able to resolve very complex problems with very simple but sleek-looking designs. And we want to really emphasize that in how we design the Polypods.”

“I think this really marks a new era for treatment innovation, where we’re able to build very large, scalable systems that use a very small amount of material and very low energy to treat very challenging contaminants,” Banks said. “And, having the first system in the world for that in Atlantic County, it’s quite unusual.”

Where PolyGone goes from here

A similar installation is already running at a wastewater plant in California, and PolyGone is developing a residential version. The Atlantic City system was fully funded by a federal grant, and both the technology and the funding route could give other municipalities a path to act without waiting on a mandate.

articles.personality_title: First wastewater plant removes microplastics with new technology
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Wastewater treatment plants clean dirty water by removing bacteria and chemicals before releasing it back into the environment. However, tiny plastic pieces called microplastics have been passing through these plants and entering oceans for years.

**What happened** – This week, a wastewater treatment plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to install a system designed to capture microplastics. The system, called Polypods, was created by two Princeton University graduates who started a company named PolyGone Systems. Their technology mimics how certain wetland plants attract and hold microplastics, removing over 98% of these tiny particles from the water.

articles.personality_title_es: La primera planta de tratamiento elimina microplásticos con nueva tecnología
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las plantas de tratamiento de aguas residuales limpian el agua al eliminar bacterias y químicos antes de devolverla al medio ambiente. Sin embargo, pequeñas piezas de plástico llamadas microplásticos han estado pasando por estas plantas y llegando a los océanos durante años.

**Qué pasó** – Esta semana, una planta de tratamiento en Atlantic City, Nueva Jersey, se convirtió en la primera en el mundo en instalar un sistema diseñado para capturar microplásticos. El sistema, llamado Polypods, fue creado por dos graduados de la Universidad de Princeton que fundaron la empresa PolyGone Systems. Su tecnología imita cómo ciertas plantas de humedales atraen y retienen microplásticos, removiendo más del 98% de estas pequeñas partículas del agua.

**Impacto** – Los microplásticos son fragmentos muy pequeños de plástico que no desaparecen y pueden acumularse dentro de animales y humanos, posiblemente causando problemas de salud. El nuevo sistema captura los microplásticos más pequeños, que son los más difíciles de eliminar y los que más fácilmente entran en los organismos vivos. Este avance ayuda a detener la contaminación plástica en los océanos y las cadenas alimenticias, protegiendo tanto el medio ambiente como la salud humana.

**Próximo paso** – PolyGone ya está instalando un sistema similar en California y trabaja en una versión para hogares. Como el proyecto de Atlantic City fue financiado por una subvención federal, otras ciudades podrían adoptar esta tecnología aunque no haya leyes que lo exijan.

**Resumen en una frase** – Por primera vez, una planta de tratamiento de aguas residuales está eliminando activamente microplásticos dañinos del agua con un nuevo sistema eficiente inspirado en la naturaleza.

articles.title: New platform aims to get money moving before disaster strikes
articles.summary: UN agencies on Thursday launched a joint platform at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, that aims to secure access to more than $3 billion in risk financing to protect 75 million people and their livelihoods from climate shocks and natural hazards by 2030.
articles.content:
“Disasters are increasingly predictable, yet the financing needed to act ahead of them remains slow and fragmented,” said Lisa Doughten, Director of Financing and Outreach at UN aid coordination office, OCHA.

The platform aims to:

make disaster response funding more predictable,

increase the money available for early action during major crises

and maximize the impact of every dollar further by combining existing resources with private sector support

Agencies will share expertise, pool data and coordinate joint solutions, pairing predictive analysis with funds so that early warnings can be turned into anticipatory action. Working with the insurance industry and financial markets will be key to keeping costs down as financing scales up.

Tweet URL

The initiative has already delivered its first results: with support from WFP’s specialist insurance teams, OCHA and UNICEF have put in place insurance policies that provide a financial safety net for their anticipatory action programmes.

“A robust forecast can give us days, sometimes even weeks, to act before a flood, storm or heatwave puts children at risk,” said Gernot Laganda, UNICEF Global Practice Director for Climate and Environment.

“Insurance ensures we have the money available to act on that warning, even in a year when several disasters come at once.”

Significant gaps

Yet pre-arranged financing still accounts for less than two per cent of global humanitarian financing, far short of what is needed.

UN emergency food agency, WFP, the UN’s largest user of such financing, has helped secure nearly $211 million in pre-arranged finance this year to protect up to 9.6 million people in more than 50 countries.

“For millions of refugees already on the frontlines of the climate crisis, acting early can save lives, protect livelihoods and prevent further displacement,” said Antón Leis García, UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Operations.

The UN Disaster Risk Financing (DRF) Platform brings together the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and the World Food Programme (WFP)
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant, coordinated UN initiative to secure over $3 billion in risk financing to protect 75 million people from climate-related disasters by 2030. This platform enhances early disaster response funding, increases predictability, and leverages private sector support, representing a meaningful advancement in climate action and humanitarian aid with broad societal impact.
articles.personality_title: UN launches platform to quickly fund disaster actions and protect millions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Climate-related disasters like floods and storms are happening more often. But money to act before these disasters strikes is often slow and scattered, making it harder to protect people.

**What happened** – At the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye, several UN agencies joined forces to create the Disaster Risk Financing (DRF) Platform. This new platform aims to secure over $3 billion by 2030 to help protect 75 million people from climate shocks and natural hazards. It combines data, expert knowledge, and funding with help from private companies and insurance to act faster and better.

**Impact** – This platform is important because it makes funding for disaster response more predictable and increases the money available to act early. For example, UNICEF and OCHA now have insurance policies that provide money quickly when a disaster warning is issued. This means they can help people days or weeks before a flood or heatwave hits, which can save lives and protect homes.

**What's next step** – The platform will keep working with financial markets and insurance companies to lower costs and raise more money. The UN agencies involved will continue to share data and coordinate actions to improve early responses. This approach could help millions more people, especially refugees and vulnerable communities, prepare for disasters in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The UN’s new platform uses smart financing and teamwork to get money moving early, helping protect millions from climate disasters before they happen.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’ONU lance une plateforme pour financer rapidement les actions avant les catastrophes et protéger des millions de personnes
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les catastrophes liées au climat, comme les inondations et les tempêtes, se produisent de plus en plus souvent. Mais l’argent pour agir avant ces catastrophes arrive souvent lentement et de manière dispersée, ce qui rend la protection des populations plus difficile.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Lors de la conférence climatique COP31 en Turquie, plusieurs agences de l’ONU se sont unies pour créer la Plateforme de financement des risques de catastrophe (DRF). Cette nouvelle plateforme vise à sécuriser plus de 3 milliards de dollars d’ici 2030 pour protéger 75 millions de personnes contre les chocs climatiques et les aléas naturels. Elle combine données, expertise et financements avec l’aide d’entreprises privées et d’assurances pour agir plus vite et mieux.

**Impact** – Cette plateforme est importante car elle rend le financement des réponses aux catastrophes plus prévisible et augmente les fonds disponibles pour agir tôt. Par exemple, l’UNICEF et le bureau de la coordination des affaires humanitaires (OCHA) disposent maintenant de polices d’assurance qui fournissent rapidement de l’argent lors d’une alerte. Cela leur permet d’aider les populations plusieurs jours, voire semaines, avant une inondation ou une vague de chaleur, ce qui peut sauver des vies et protéger des maisons.

**Prochaine étape** – La plateforme continuera de travailler avec les marchés financiers et les compagnies d’assurance pour réduire les coûts et mobiliser plus d’argent. Les agences de l’ONU impliquées partageront toujours leurs données et coordonneront leurs actions pour améliorer les réponses précoces. Cette approche pourrait aider des millions de personnes supplémentaires, notamment les réfugiés et les communautés vulnérables, à se préparer aux catastrophes à venir.

**Phrase clé** – La nouvelle plateforme de l’ONU utilise un financement intelligent et la coopération pour faire circuler l’argent rapidement, aidant à protéger des millions de personnes des catastrophes climatiques avant qu’elles ne surviennent.
articles.personality_title_es: La ONU lanza una plataforma para financiar rápidamente acciones antes de desastres y proteger a millones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los desastres relacionados con el clima, como inundaciones y tormentas, ocurren cada vez más. Pero el dinero para actuar antes de estos desastres suele ser lento y disperso, dificultando la protección de las personas.

**Qué pasó** – En la conferencia climática COP31 en Turquía, varias agencias de la ONU unieron fuerzas para crear la Plataforma de Financiamiento para Riesgos de Desastres (DRF). Esta nueva plataforma busca asegurar más de 3 mil millones de dólares para 2030 y proteger a 75 millones de personas de choques climáticos y peligros naturales. Combina datos, conocimientos expertos y financiamiento con ayuda del sector privado y seguros para actuar más rápido y mejor.

articles.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.
articles.content:
A butterfly commonly seen throughout Central and South America has been concealing a remarkable secret. For more than two centuries, scientists believed that the genus Colobura contained just one widespread species. Now, researchers have identified a third species that looks almost identical to its relatives, raising new questions about how these butterflies evolved and continue to live alongside one another.

The newly identified species, named Colobura cryptica, was described in the journal Zootaxa by researchers led by Anisha Sapkota, a doctoral student at the Florida Museum of Natural History. By combining DNA analysis with subtle differences in wing patterns and ultraviolet light reflection, the team uncovered distinctions that had remained largely invisible to scientists.

Even more surprising, the three species occupy overlapping regions and can be found in the same places at the same time. Yet genetic evidence suggests they remain separate, with no detectable signs of interbreeding.

A Familiar Butterfly With a Hidden Identity

Central and South America's tropical rainforests contain some of the greatest concentrations of biodiversity on the planet. Costa Rica alone supports approximately half a million species, roughly five times the number found across Canada, even though Canada's land area is about 200 times larger.

Despite this extraordinary diversity, certain plants and animals are especially recognizable throughout the region. In Canada's boreal forests, balsam firs are a familiar feature of the landscape. In tropical America, trees belonging to the genus Cecropia play a similarly prominent role.

In 1888, German botanist Andreas Schimper described their importance, writing, "Every naturalist who has been in tropical America will remember Cecropia, belonging to the most conspicuous trees of those countries."

The butterflies of the genus Colobura are just as recognizable, according to Sapkota.

"If you go to the neotropics, Colobura is one of the first butterflies you see," she said.

These butterflies and Cecropia trees share a close ecological relationship because Cecropia leaves provide food for Colobura caterpillars. Both groups occur across an enormous geographic area, from portions of the Andes Mountains and the Brazilian Amazon to the Atlantic Rainforest in Brazil and Paraguay. They are also widespread throughout Central America and the Caribbean Islands.

Such broad distributions are not particularly unusual in tropical ecosystems. However, the diversity within these groups presents an interesting contrast.

Scientists recognize 61 species of Cecropia, many of which occupy relatively small geographic areas. Some grow only in the Andes, while others are confined to the Caribbean.

For Colobura butterflies, the situation appeared very different. After Carl Linnaeus formally described Colobura dirce in 1758, scientists spent more than 200 years treating the genus as a single species, despite its extensive range.

That understanding began to change in 2001, when researchers formally recognized a second species. Now, an unexpected discovery in Venezuela has led to the identification of a third, described by Sapkota and her colleagues in Zootaxa.

Rather than providing a simple explanation for the group's evolutionary history, the discovery has introduced an even greater puzzle.

"It's crazy to think about. These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time."

A Butterfly Mystery Dating Back More Than 150 Years

Distinguishing adult Colobura butterflies is exceptionally difficult. Their wings are nearly identical, with only slight variations in a gray stripe on the underside of the front wings. In some butterflies, this stripe becomes a little wider. In others, it stays the same width. It may also extend far enough to meet a yellow band running across the wing, or stop short of it.

Their caterpillars offer somewhat clearer clues.

Colobura caterpillars have velvety black bodies covered with prominent yellow projections that end in sharply angled barbs. These defensive structures send a warning to potential predators that could be interpreted as "leave me alone, or there will be unpleasant consequences."

Beneath those conspicuous spines are much smaller cream-colored markings. Depending on the species, these markings may resemble teardrops or rings, or they may be missing entirely.

The importance of these differences was recognized surprisingly early.

In 1852, Dutch entomologist Jan Sepp proposed that caterpillars with different cream-colored patterns represented two separate species. Other researchers rejected his interpretation, arguing that the variations could reflect differences between males and females or simply natural variation within a single species.

That view remained dominant for approximately 150 years.

In 2001, Keith Willmott and several colleagues revisited Sepp's observations and formally described a second species, Colobura annulata. Willmott is now a curator at the Florida Museum's McGuire Center for Lepidoptera and Biodiversity.

"We assumed that was the problem solved," Willmott said.

He moved on to other research, believing the longstanding classification problem had been resolved. However, occasional observations continued to suggest that something was missing.

"I had a few indications that there was a third species, but I thought it was too implausible."

At the time, even the existence of two nearly indistinguishable species seemed remarkable.

"It's a very distinctive butterfly. It's hard to imagine there being two species in the same area that look alike because they're so different from anything else."

An Unexpected Discovery in Venezuela

Roughly 25 years later, fresh evidence emerged when Willmott's colleague Andrés Orellana encountered a group of hungry Colobura caterpillars feeding on a young Cecropia tree in Venezuela.

The caterpillars were rapidly stripping leaves from the sapling. They possessed the familiar black body segments near the head and yellow spines characteristic of the genus, but one feature stood out.

Unlike the two recognized species, these caterpillars had no cream-colored markings at all.

Orellana photographed the unusual insects and shared the images with Willmott. The discovery provided a compelling reason to investigate whether a third species had been overlooked.

Sapkota had recently joined the Shirey lab at the Florida Museum and was eager to lead the investigation.

Working with her colleagues, she designed a study that combined genetic evidence with careful examinations of butterfly anatomy.

First, she studied DNA barcodes, short and highly variable genetic sequences that help researchers distinguish species. These sequences came from a long-running survey of butterflies and moths in Costa Rica led by study co-authors Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs.

The investigation then expanded to older butterfly specimens collected across tropical Central and South America. Sapkota sent these museum samples to Nick Grishin at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, where researchers sequenced both their mitochondrial and nuclear genomes.

The genetic results provided a way to test whether the butterflies represented genuinely different evolutionary groups rather than ordinary variations within a single species.

But the researchers also wanted to know whether there were physical differences that previous scientists had failed to notice.

An Invisible Clue Hidden in Butterfly Wings

Sapkota spent hours examining preserved butterflies in museum collections, searching for consistent traits that might distinguish the suspected species.

At first, the effort produced few answers. Other than the slight differences in the gray wing stripe, the butterflies appeared remarkably similar.

Eventually, she noticed something unusual.

The undersides of some wings appeared to have a faint violet shimmer, and the intensity of that sheen seemed to vary between specimens.

This observation suggested that the insects might reflect ultraviolet light, which falls outside the range of human vision but can be detected by many butterflies.

"I checked it with a spectrometer and found that even though the butterflies didn't look violet to me, it reflected UV light," she said.

The measurements revealed a striking pattern. All three species reflected ultraviolet light, but the wavelengths differed.

The researchers named the newly identified species Colobura cryptica, reflecting its previously concealed identity.

Although the visible differences were extremely subtle, the ultraviolet measurements, caterpillar markings, and DNA results told a consistent story.

The three species could be distinguished by the following features:

Species Adult wing characteristics Average UV reflectance Caterpillar markings Colobura dirce Gray band widens slightly and does not reach the yellow crossband 376 nm Cream-colored teardrops on abdominal segments Colobura annulata Gray band stays uniform in width and meets the yellow crossband 370 nm Cream-colored rings on abdominal segments Colobura cryptica Gray band stays uniform in width but does not meet the yellow crossband 344 nm No cream-colored markings

There is an additional complication with Colobura dirce. It includes two subspecies with different ultraviolet reflectance values. Colobura dirce dirce reflects light at 362.2 nm, while Colobura dirce wolcotti reflects light at 390.6 nm. The 376 nm value represents the average for the species.

Beyond these minor wing differences, Sapkota could not identify any other consistent anatomical distinctions. Even the male genitalia, which often provide some of the most reliable features for separating butterfly and moth species, appeared indistinguishable.

Nevertheless, the genetic findings were decisive.

DNA analysis identified three distinct evolutionary lineages, and those divisions matched the physical differences the team had documented. Together, the evidence confirmed that Colobura contains three species rather than two.

Three Butterfly Species Living Side by Side

Identifying a previously unknown butterfly species is significant on its own, but the geographic distributions of these three species make the finding particularly intriguing.

All three occur in overlapping portions of Central and South America.

Colobura dirce has the widest distribution, extending from Mexico to southeastern Brazil. It occurs on both sides of the Andes Mountains and throughout the Caribbean archipelago.

Colobura annulata also occupies a large geographic area, although it is absent from the Greater Antilles.

The newly described Colobura cryptica has the smallest known range, stretching from southern Mexico to the foothills of the Andes.

These overlapping distributions raise an important evolutionary question. How did three species become genetically distinct while continuing to occupy many of the same regions?

Species often emerge when populations become isolated from one another. A mountain range, for example, might divide a population and prevent individuals on opposite sides from mating.

Over many generations, the separated groups can accumulate different genetic and physical traits. If those differences become great enough, the populations may eventually lose the ability to interbreed, even if they come into contact again.

But geographic separation is not the only mechanism that can drive the formation of new species.

Researchers suspect that the Colobura butterflies might have developed different ways of using their shared forest habitats.

"There could be vertical stratification between these butterflies," Sapkota said. "Colobura dirce is typically found in the undergrowth and C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in the canopy, but we do not know for sure because there have been mixed signals coming from different studies."

In other words, one species may spend more time near the forest floor while the others favor the upper branches.

This kind of habitat separation could potentially help maintain differences between species living in the same geographic area.

However, previous research has produced inconsistent observations. One reason may be that even experienced butterfly specialists have difficulty telling the three species apart.

How Do Nearly Identical Butterflies Recognize Each Other?

An even more puzzling question concerns how the butterflies identify suitable mates.

Many moths and some butterflies use special scent glands to release pheromones, chemical signals that help individuals recognize members of their own species.

Colobura butterflies lack those glands.

That suggests visual information may play an important role in mate selection. Yet their nearly identical appearance makes it difficult to understand how they distinguish one species from another.

The newly discovered ultraviolet differences offer a possible explanation.

Although humans cannot see ultraviolet light, many butterflies can. Sapkota suspects that the different ultraviolet reflections from their wings might provide visual signals that help them identify members of their own species.

Similar mechanisms are known or suspected in other butterflies and moths. Garden whites, sulfur butterflies, and wood tiger moths possess ultraviolet-reflecting wing scales that researchers believe may contribute to mate selection.

Sapkota is investigating whether Colobura butterflies use comparable signals, but the results have not yet provided a clear answer.

Whatever mechanism they use, the butterflies appear remarkably successful at maintaining their separate identities.

Analysis of nuclear DNA found no evidence of hybridization among the three species, despite their overlapping ranges.

The findings suggest that the species have followed separate evolutionary paths without detectable genetic mixing.

A Familiar Butterfly Still Holds Many Secrets

The discovery of Colobura cryptica demonstrates how much remains unknown about even widespread, conspicuous animals.

For generations, naturalists studied these butterflies without recognizing the full diversity hidden within the group. Only by combining detailed observations with modern genetic testing and ultraviolet measurements were researchers able to uncover the third species.

Yet some of the most important questions remain unanswered, including how the butterflies choose mates, whether they occupy different parts of the forest, and what originally caused their evolutionary separation.

For Sapkota, answering those questions will require observing the insects in their natural habitats.

"Someone has to go the field to find it out themselves."

Those interested in another unusual aspect of Colobura biology can explore the Biodiversity Heritage Library, which contains a whimsical account published in 1952 describing the poop perches that young Colobura caterpillars construct during their earliest developmental stages.

Study Authors and Funding

Additional study co-authors include Andrés Orellana of the Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira; Nick Grishin and Leina Song of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; Isidro Chacón of the Museo Nacional Santo Domingo de Heredia; Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs of the University of Pennsylvania; and Sajan KC of the Florida Museum of Natural History.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Welch Foundation, Canada's New Frontiers in Research Fund (NFRFt-2020- 00073), the Canada Foundation for Innovation's Major Science Infrastructure program (MSI 42450), BioAlfa, and Project UNET (Universidad Nacional Experimental del Táchira).

articles.personality_title: Scientists discover a hidden third butterfly species after 200 years
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For over 200 years, scientists believed that a tropical butterfly called Colobura was just one species living across Central and South America. These butterflies are common and easy to spot in rainforests, and their caterpillars feed on Cecropia trees. 

**What happened** – Researchers led by Anisha Sapkota at the Florida Museum of Natural History found that what was thought to be one species is actually three. They used DNA tests and noticed subtle differences in the butterflies’ wing patterns, especially in how the wings reflect ultraviolet (UV) light, which humans can’t see but butterflies can. One of these species, named Colobura cryptica, was completely unknown until now.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because the three butterfly species live in the same places and look almost identical, yet they do not interbreed. This challenges common ideas about how species form and stay separate. It also shows how much we still have to learn about animals that seem familiar. The UV wing patterns might help butterflies recognize their own kind, a clue to how they avoid mixing with other species.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to study these butterflies in their natural habitats to understand how they choose mates and if they live in different parts of the forest, such as near the ground or in the tree canopy. This could explain how they stay separate despite living close together. Further research may also reveal more hidden species or new facts about butterfly evolution.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After 200 years, scientists revealed that a common tropical butterfly is actually three nearly identical species, using DNA and hidden ultraviolet wing patterns to uncover their secret identities.

articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Pendant plus de 200 ans, les scientifiques pensaient qu’un papillon tropical appelé Colobura était une seule espèce vivant en Amérique centrale et du Sud. Ces papillons sont courants dans les forêts tropicales, et leurs chenilles se nourrissent des feuilles des arbres Cecropia.

L’une de ces espèces, nommée Colobura cryptica, était totalement inconnue.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car ces trois espèces vivent dans les mêmes endroits et se ressemblent presque parfaitement, mais ne s’hybrident pas. Cela remet en question les idées habituelles sur la formation et la séparation des espèces. Cela montre aussi combien nous ignorons encore sur des animaux familiers. **Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques veulent observer ces papillons dans leur habitat naturel pour comprendre comment ils choisissent leurs partenaires et s’ils vivent dans différentes parties de la forêt, comme près du sol ou dans la canopée. Cela pourrait expliquer comment ils restent séparés malgré leur proximité. D’autres recherches pourraient aussi révéler d’autres espèces cachées ou de nouvelles informations sur l’évolution des papillons.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren una tercera especie de mariposa oculta durante 200 años
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante más de 200 años, los científicos creyeron que una mariposa tropical llamada Colobura era una sola especie que vivía en América Central y del Sur. Estas mariposas son comunes en las selvas tropicales, y sus orugas se alimentan de árboles Cecropia.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores liderados por Anisha Sapkota en el Florida Museum of Natural History descubrieron que lo que pensaban que era una especie en realidad son tres. Usaron pruebas de ADN y notaron diferencias sutiles en los patrones de las alas, especialmente en cómo reflejan la luz ultravioleta (UV), que los humanos no podemos ver pero las mariposas sí. Una de estas especies, llamada Colobura cryptica, era desconocida hasta ahora.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque las tres especies viven en los mismos lugares y se ven casi iguales, pero no se cruzan entre ellas. Esto desafía las ideas comunes sobre cómo se forman y mantienen separadas las especies. También muestra cuánto queda por aprender sobre animales que parecen familiares. Los patrones UV podrían ayudar a las mariposas a reconocer a las de su propia especie.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren estudiar estas mariposas en su hábitat natural para entender cómo eligen pareja y si viven en diferentes partes del bosque, como cerca del suelo o en la copa de los árboles. Esto podría explicar cómo permanecen separadas a pesar de vivir juntas. Más investigaciones podrían revelar más especies ocultas o nuevos datos sobre la evolución de las mariposas.

**Una frase clave** – Después de 200 años, los científicos revelaron que una mariposa tropical común es en realidad tres especies casi idénticas, usando ADN y patrones ocultos en luz ultravioleta para descubrir sus identidades secretas.
